findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify, in the plan, the blocking vs advisory classification for each named signal (config-applied, config-valid, llm-provider, github, deploy-host/replication, environment), or state the default rule (e.g. 'all signals blocking unless explicitly marked advisory').
evidence: Plan lists six named signals (config-applied, config-valid, llm-provider, github, deploy-host/replication, environment) without assigning each a blocking or advisory classification.
AC2 relies on a blocking signal being unhealthy, but the test cannot be deterministically written without knowing which signals are blocking.
This is signal (1) undefined scope boundary and signal (6) ambiguous priority — which signals block vs advise is essential, not nice-to-have.
findings.finding: The plan names 'per-signal blocking vs advisory severity' as a core aggregator design but never specifies WHICH signals (config-applied, config-valid, llm-provider, github, deploy-host/replication, environment) are classified as blocking vs advisory. This is a load-bearing design decision that directly controls whether submit is blocked, yet it is deferred to the executor.
findings.location: DESIGN section, Aggregator bullet: 'per-signal blocking vs advisory severity; fail-closed on any blocking-unhealthy'
scenarios: An implementer could reasonably classify 'deploy-host/replication' as advisory (not blocking), shipping a system that fails open on replication lag — contradicting the PRINCIPLE.
A test author writing AC2 cannot construct a valid blocking-signal scenario without knowing the classification table.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a signal classification table in the DESIGN section. Example default: all signals are blocking except 'environment' which is advisory until proven reliable, with the table being the canonical source for AC2 test construction.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document (or design around) the bootstrapping ordering constraint: enabling the Infra-Ready Gerrit submit-requirement requires a manual project.config apply (currently detect-only); the plan should specify the deployment sequence so the gate doesn't require the same class of untracked manual work it is meant to prevent.
evidence: infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh line 98-107: 'CONFIG_PATHS=...infra/gerrit/project.config...' and 'config paths are DETECT-ONLY in v1 (signalled, never auto-applied)'
Plan: 'LANDING boundary — dedicated bot-cast Infra-Ready submit-requirement blocks submit with an explicit per-signal message'
A new submit-requirement requires editing infra/gerrit/project.config and applying it via a manual operator step — the same class of work the plan's gate is designed to track and guard.
findings.finding: The plan proposes adding a new Infra-Ready Gerrit submit-requirement, but Gerrit project.config changes are currently on CONFIG_PATHS (detect-only, never auto-applied in the unattended deploy loop). The plan doesn't address this bootstrapping dependency: enabling the Infra-Ready gate requires a config apply that the existing system explicitly refuses to automate. This creates a chicken-and-egg: the gate can't go live without a manual operator apply that is itself in the class of work the gate is meant to guard.
findings.location: DESIGN section: 'LANDING boundary — dedicated bot-cast Infra-Ready submit-requirement blocks submit'
scenarios: The Infra-Ready gate is designed but cannot be enabled because enabling it requires a project.config apply that is intentionally not automated.

An operator manually applies project.config to add the submit-requirement, but the gate then immediately blocks all submits because infra-health signals are still bootstrapping (WARN mode), creating a live-site incident.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit 'Deployment pre-requisite' section specifying: (1) deploy health registry + signals in WARN mode first (no config change required); (2) only after signals are proven reliable, perform the project.config apply to add the submit-requirement; (3) simultaneously flip to fail-closed. Alternatively, if the Infra-Ready gate is implemented as a bot-cast vote on an EXISTING label rather than a new submit-requirement, no config change is needed.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify whether the 'infra-class retry loop' on signal recovery IS the existing reconciler (triggered early on health-state transition) or a new parallel path; if a new path, specify how it shares the existing single-flight lock, dedup ledger, and attempt-budget counter to avoid double-trigger and budget inconsistency.
evidence: src/rebar/review_bot/adapter.py:62: RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS = frozenset({'review-error', 'llm-unavailable', 'scanner', 'gate-disabled'})
src/rebar/review_bot/reconcile.py: reconcile_loop already re-drives vote-less changes on the SAME patchset
src/rebar/review_bot/voter.py:436-452: per-(change_id, revision) asyncio.Lock and dedup store already serialize concurrent review attempts
Plan proposes a separate 'infra-class retry loop' triggered by signal recovery — a second recovery driver alongside the reconciler
findings.finding: The plan's 'auto-re-run blocked reviews on recovery' mechanism is not adequately differentiated from the existing retryable-gap + reconciler backfill path (RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS / reconcile_loop). The existing mechanism already handles llm-unavailable, review-error, scanner, and gate-disabled by leaving the change vote-less and letting the reconciler re-drive it. Adding a second, independently-triggered recovery path for the same changes creates a potential double-trigger: both the new 'signal-recovery' loop and the existing reconciler may enqueue the same (change_id, revision) concurrently, and the plan does not specify whether the new path shares or bypasses the existing single-flight lock and dedup ledger.
findings.location: DESIGN section: 'Recovery = infra-class retry loop: on signal recovery, auto-re-run blocked reviews + re-eval gate; bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd), same-patchset re-vote that cleanly REPLACES the stale -1'
scenarios: Signal recovers; both the new recovery loop and the next reconciler tick independently enqueue the same 10 vote-less changes. The dedup lock serializes them, but the queue fills with double entries, and the single worker processes each change twice (the second as a dedup skip, wasting queue capacity).
The new recovery loop uses a different retry budget counter than the existing DedupStore.record_attempt, causing the RETRY_LIMIT to be applied inconsistently.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how the tri-state health registry integrates with or supersedes the existing mirror_guard.py binary verdict schema, including how mirror_guard's exit-2 (IO error) maps to the 'unknown' (not 'unhealthy') tri-state to preserve the no-false-clear invariant.
evidence: mirror_guard.py line 17: 'Verdict schema (both checks): {"check": str, "healthy": bool, "reason": str, ...}'
mirror_guard.py lines 55, 63, 83, 109–113: binary healthy/unhealthy verdicts, no tri-state/unknown
Plan DESIGN: 'Health registry: named checks, each tri-state healthy/unhealthy/unknown (never conflate check errored with healthy)'
ABSENCE: plan text contains no reference to mirror_guard, its existing verdict schema, or how it maps to the proposed registry
findings.finding: The plan proposes a new tri-state health registry covering 'github (API/Actions/mirror)' and 'deploy-host/replication' signals, but the codebase already contains mirror_guard.py which implements replication-divergence and ruleset-drift checks in a binary {"healthy": bool} schema. The plan does not acknowledge this existing implementation or specify whether the health registry wraps, supersedes, or must reconcile with mirror_guard's binary verdict schema — risking a parallel/duplicate health implementation or an incompatible signal contract.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'Signals: config-applied … github (API/Actions/mirror), deploy-host/replication'
scenarios: Implementation team builds a new github/replication probe duplicating mirror_guard logic, resulting in two divergent health signals for the same underlying condition.

The tri-state registry wraps mirror_guard but must translate binary {healthy: bool} to tri-state — if mirror_guard throws an exception it returns exit-code 2 (error), but the registry must not conflate that with 'unhealthy' vs 'unknown'. Without explicit guidance this mapping is ambiguous.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a subsection under DESIGN (or a named story) stating that mirror_guard probes are wrapped by a tri-state adapter: exit-0 all-healthy → healthy, exit-1 any-unhealthy → unhealthy, exit-2 IO error → unknown. This is the only mapping that satisfies the plan's own 'probe error never returns healthy' rule.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify how the new infra health registry relates to the existing review_bot /health endpoint: specify whether registry signals are merged into /health (with schema versioning), exposed on a separate endpoint, or served via a different mechanism — and confirm that the existing drain-loop in_flight semantics are preserved.
evidence: src/rebar/review_bot/app.py:245-246: existing @app.get('/health') endpoint already live
src/rebar/review_bot/voter.py:55-71: in_flight counter exported via /health, used by deploy loop's deferral logic
voter.py:715: 'unenforces the drain and per-review wait_for bounds and stalls /health'
ABSENCE: plan does not mention the existing /health endpoint or its drain-loop consumers
findings.finding: The review_bot already has a /health endpoint (app.py:245) used for drain-orchestration (in_flight count, per voter.py comments). The plan introduces a 'health registry' as if starting from scratch and does not address whether this new registry extends the existing /health endpoint, replaces it, or runs as a separate side-channel. Omitting this relationship risks the new registry being built in parallel rather than integrating with the existing operational health surface, or inadvertently breaking the drain-loop that depends on the current /health semantics.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'Health registry: named checks' / 'Consumption points'
scenarios: New infra-health registry signals are surfaced on a separate endpoint or internal object, while the existing /health endpoint continues serving only in_flight, creating two divergent operator-facing health surfaces.
An implementation change to /health to add registry signals inadvertently alters the JSON schema the deploy loop polls, breaking autodeploy health gating.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify whether the infra-health abstain path introduces a new `gap_reason` entry into `_TAG_SUFFIXES` and `RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS` (making it a vote-less defer recoverable by the existing reconciler) or takes a distinct no-vote path, and ensure this decision rule is co-located with those schema definitions.
evidence: adapter.py:62: RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS = frozenset({'review-error', 'llm-unavailable', 'scanner', 'gate-disabled'})
retrigger.py:64: _GAP_RE = re.compile(r'^BLOCK — coverage-gap \((?P<reason>[a-z][a-z-]*)\)$') — this regex must match any new gap_reason for retrigger to classify it correctly.

Plan says 'no content vote' but current voter.py:600–632 has two paths for coverage gaps: vote-less defer (if gap_reason in RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS and under budget) or immediate -1 escalation. The plan does not specify which path the new infra-health abstain takes.
findings.finding: The plan says the review-bot 'ABSTAINS (casts no LLM-Review content vote) when infra unhealthy', but does not specify how this interacts with the existing `_TAG_SUFFIXES` enum (adapter.py:44) and `RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS` frozenset (adapter.py:62), nor whether a new infra-health-gate gap_reason is added to that frozenset so the existing retrigger.py parser (`classify_tag`, `_GAP_RE`) and the bounded retry budget (`retryable_gap_max_attempts`) recognize it correctly.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'REVIEW boundary — review-bot ABSTAINS (casts no LLM-Review content vote) when infra unhealthy'; adapter.py:44–62; retrigger.py:60–64
scenarios: A new 'infra-not-ready' gap_reason is introduced but not added to RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS — the voter immediately casts a -1 instead of deferring, defeating the abstain intent.
The classify_tag parser in retrigger.py sees an unrecognized gap_reason body and returns 'unparseable', blocking contributor-triggered re-review via recheck-review.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Revise AC3 to verify the full bounded-retry contract: assert that recovery triggers re-runs up to RETRY_LIMIT (not 'exactly one'), and that the loop terminates correctly on limit exhaustion.
evidence: AC3: 'asserts exactly one bounded re-run'
Design: 'bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd)' — implies a loop capable of multiple attempts
findings.finding: AC3 constrains verification to 'exactly one bounded re-run', but the plan body describes a bounded retry loop with RETRY_LIMIT (implying up to N retries, not exactly one). The verify step measures a narrower behavior than the deliverable specifies, leaving the multi-retry path untested by any criterion.
findings.location: AC3 ('verified by a test that drives unhealthy then healthy and asserts exactly one bounded re-run') vs. Design section ('bounded (RETRY_LIMIT)')
scenarios: A test passing 'exactly one re-run' would not catch a bug where the retry counter is not decremented correctly on subsequent outages.
The RETRY_LIMIT exhaustion path (leading to 'terminal alert') is untestable if the AC is read as requiring exactly one retry.
findings.suggested_fix: Change AC3 verification language to: 'verified by a test that drives repeated unhealthy→healthy cycles and asserts re-runs are bounded by RETRY_LIMIT, with no further re-run attempted after exhaustion.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC (or extend AC6) to verify that an unauthorized actor's waiver attempt is rejected, confirming the guard-the-guard / Gatekeeper authorization check is enforced.
evidence: Design: 'guard-the-guard on who may waive (Gatekeeper)'
AC6: 'exercising the waiver path and asserting the audit record is written' — no assertion about authorization rejection
findings.finding: The plan body describes 'guard-the-guard on who may waive (Gatekeeper)' as a distinct authorization mechanism, but no AC covers this authorization check. AC6 only verifies that 'the audit record is written', not that unauthorized actors are prevented from issuing waivers.
findings.location: Design section ('Waiver + break-glass: audited per-signal/global override; guard-the-guard on who may waive (Gatekeeper)') vs. AC6
scenarios: An unprivileged actor issuing a waiver would bypass the gate; the AC6 test would still pass because it only checks audit-record creation, not authorization enforcement.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC that covers the terminal-alert-on-exhaustion behavior: verify that when RETRY_LIMIT is reached, an alert is emitted to the configured channel (not silently dropped).
evidence: Design: 'bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd), same-patchset re-vote … terminal alert on exhaustion'
ABSENCE: no AC mentions alerting, notification, or behavior after RETRY_LIMIT is reached
findings.finding: The plan body specifies 'terminal alert on exhaustion' (when RETRY_LIMIT is reached) as an explicit deliverable, but no AC covers this behavior.
findings.location: Design section ('terminal alert on exhaustion') vs. AC set
scenarios: A misconfigured alerting path (wrong channel, silent failure) would go undetected because no acceptance test exercises or asserts the terminal-alert output.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC that covers advisory-severity signals: verify that an unhealthy advisory signal emits a message without blocking submit or suppressing the content vote.
evidence: Design: 'per-signal blocking vs advisory severity; fail-closed on any blocking-unhealthy'
ABSENCE: all ACs address blocking signals; none assert that advisory signals do not block submit or suppress content votes
findings.finding: The plan body describes 'per-signal blocking vs advisory severity' signals — where advisory signals are emitted but do not block. No AC covers the advisory-severity signal path, leaving its behavior (emit-without-block) unverified.
findings.location: Design section ('Aggregator: per-signal blocking vs advisory severity') vs. AC set
scenarios: A regression that accidentally elevates an advisory signal to blocking would not be caught by any mandated test.
An advisory signal that silently stops emitting would equally go undetected.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Each child that owns a parent AC must carry an explicit acceptance-criteria item or verify_command reproducing the 'verified by a test that...' clause from the parent.
evidence: Parent AC1: 'verified by a unit test that feeds an errored probe and asserts the aggregate is unknown, not healthy'
Parent AC2: 'verified by an offline test asserting no content vote is emitted and submit is blocked'
Parent AC3: 'verified by a test that drives unhealthy then healthy and asserts exactly one bounded re-run'
Parent AC4: 'verified by a test that presents a stale-revision observation and asserts rejection'
Parent AC5: 'verified by a test asserting detect-only emits signals without blocking and the flip enables blocking'
Parent AC6: 'verified by a test exercising the waiver path and asserting the audit record is written'
All 8 child tickets: verify_commands=[], no structured acceptance criteria in any ticket body — only description prose
findings.finding: No child carries the explicit test/verification clause required by the parent ACs. All six parent acceptance criteria include a 'verified by a test that...' specification; every child ticket has only a prose description, no verify_commands, and no structured acceptance criteria. The observable test outcomes (e.g., 'feeds an errored probe and asserts the aggregate is unknown', 'asserts exactly one bounded re-run', 'asserts the audit record is written') are unowned by any child.
findings.location: child d0fb-7404-0665-4a65, child 571e-f50b-c337-49ae, child acdb-2b03-0b2d-49bd, child e75e-0740-4642-434f, child fad7-8c63-18f2-4db5, child a0d0-7098-ea0e-4327, child 1028-9767-365c-423e, child 1de6-30b9-2e32-4223
scenarios: Completion verifier checks parent ACs against child deliverables: no child produces the required test artifacts, so the parent is structurally unverifiable.
A child delivers the behavioral code but not the test; the parent AC is declared done without evidence, causing a false-pass at integration.
findings.suggested_fix: Add structured acceptance criteria (with verify_commands) to each child that directly owns a parent AC, specifying the exact test assertion the parent requires. E.g., S1 should include: 'unit test feeds a probe that raises an exception and asserts registry.aggregate() == UNKNOWN'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] One child (S3 or S4, or a dedicated integration story) must own the joint offline test asserting both no-content-vote and submit-blocked in a single test scenario.
evidence: Parent AC2: 'verified by an offline test asserting no content vote is emitted and submit is blocked' — single test covering both outcomes
S4 description: 'when unhealthy it ABSTAINS — casts no LLM-Review content vote' — covers first half only
S3 description: 'blocks submit fail-closed with an explicit PER-SIGNAL message when infra unhealthy' — covers second half only
No sibling declares ownership of an integration test combining both assertions simultaneously
findings.finding: Parent AC2 requires one 'offline test asserting no content vote is emitted AND submit is blocked' as a joint assertion. S4 (review-boundary abstain) and S3 (landing-boundary submit-requirement) each own one half but neither names the other as a prerequisite for a joint integration test. No child owns the combined test, creating a partial-without-remainder gap.
findings.location: child e75e-0740-4642-434f (S4), child acdb-2b03-0b2d-49bd (S3)
scenarios: S3 and S4 each pass their own isolated tests but the integration scenario (abstain fires, submit also blocked) is never exercised, masking a coordination bug where the abstain doesn't properly propagate to the landing gate.
findings.suggested_fix: Assign the joint integration test to S3 (it is the later-executing gate and already depends on S1); add an AC: 'offline test drives the full path: unhealthy signal → review-bot abstains (no LLM-Review vote cast) AND Infra-Ready submit-requirement blocks submit with per-signal message'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] S7 (1028-9767-365c-423e) must specify that each additional signal's observation is also bound to a config/probe revision, and that stale observations are rejected — not only for the config-applied signal in S2.
evidence: Parent AC4: 'each health observation is bound to the config revision it was computed against'
S2 (a0d0) description: 'bound to the config revision it was computed against (Terraform stale-plan rejection)' — scoped to config-applied signal only

S7 (1028) description: 'llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota), github (API/Actions/mirror), config-valid, deploy-host/replication, environment. Each an independent tri-state probe with blocking/advisory severity.' — no mention of revision-binding for any of these signals
S1 (d0fb) description: no mention of revision-binding requirement in framework
findings.finding: Parent AC4 ('each health observation is bound to the config revision it was computed against and a stale observation is rejected') is scope-narrowed: S2 covers revision-binding for the config-applied signal only, while S7 introduces five additional signals (LLM-provider, GitHub, config-valid, deploy-host/replication, environment) with no requirement that these also be revision-bound. No other sibling covers the remainder.
scenarios: LLM-provider or GitHub health observations computed against an old config revision are accepted, allowing a stale-healthy status to false-clear a blocking gate.
The stale-plan rejection pattern is not enforced for signals beyond config-applied, violating the parent's 'each' qualifier.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend S1's framework to carry a revision-token on every probe result (not just config-applied), and add an AC to S7 requiring that each new signal implementation uses the same stale-rejection mechanism.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify whether the infra-class auto-recovery RETRY_LIMIT reuses the existing `review_attempts` / `retryable_gap_max_attempts` budget or introduces a separate counter, and describe how re-arm interacts with the existing bb9b contributor re-trigger reset.
evidence: dedup.py:34–41 shows the existing `review_attempts` table with `(change_id, revision, attempts, last_attempt_at)` as the counter store.
retrigger.py:24: 'On acceptance the 0347 retry budget is re-armed (reset_attempts — the row DELETE) before the forced re-review is enqueued'.

Plan does not state whether RETRY_LIMIT == retryable_gap_max_attempts or is a new independent limit, nor where the windowed thundering-herd counter increments relative to the existing attempt counter.
findings.finding: The plan's 'bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd)' recovery loop for infra-class auto-retry does not specify whether it reuses or is separate from the existing `DedupStore.review_attempts` counter and `retryable_gap_max_attempts` config already in the codebase, nor how the re-arm (reset_attempts DELETE) interacts with the bb9b contributor re-trigger that already resets the same budget.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'Recovery = infra-class retry loop: on signal recovery, auto-re-run blocked reviews + re-eval gate; bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd), same-patchset re-vote that cleanly REPLACES the stale -1'
scenarios: Implementation adds a second counter table for infra-recovery retries — now two counters compete and their re-arm semantics conflict.
The infra-recovery re-run increments the existing attempt counter, burning the bounded budget and blocking a subsequent contributor recheck-review.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the unverified capability assertion for the Anthropic health probe: specify the concrete probe mechanism (e.g., Anthropic status page poll, cheap inference canary call with quota-error classification, or SDK error-code interception at request time) and document whether quota headroom is distinguishable from reachability at probe time.
evidence: Plan text: 'llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)' listed as a named health signal with no probe specification
ABSENCE: no reference to Anthropic status page, SDK health check method, or quota API in the plan
Anthropic does not publish a machine-readable public status/quota endpoint comparable to, e.g., AWS Health API or GitHub's status.github.com
findings.finding: The plan lists 'llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)' as a named blocking health signal without specifying the probe mechanism. Anthropic does not publish a documented public health/status endpoint; quota exhaustion is only observable at inference-request time, not as an out-of-band probe. This is an unverified capability assertion — the plan asserts this signal can be obtained but does not ground it in a known API or fallback strategy.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'Signals: … llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)'
scenarios: Implementation discovers there is no out-of-band Anthropic quota probe, so the check degrades to 'make a cheap test call' — which itself consumes quota and adds latency to every review boundary check.
The probe is implemented as a TCP/HTTPS reachability check to api.anthropic.com, which passes even during quota exhaustion, producing a false-healthy signal.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Identify and verify the specific Anthropic API endpoint (or minimal inference call shape) that will serve as the llm-provider liveness probe; confirm whether a quota-headroom signal is obtainable without a full inference call and document the probe mechanism in the plan.
evidence: Plan text: 'llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)' named as a health check signal
src/rebar/llm/anthropic_model.py: existing Anthropic integration is call-only (no probe/health endpoint used)
No /health or /status endpoint exists in Anthropic's published API surface (Unverified — no documented public probe endpoint found in codebase or training knowledge)
Evidence class: Unverified — the specific probe endpoint/mechanism is unconfirmed
findings.finding: The plan asserts a named 'llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)' health signal but does not identify a specific Anthropic API endpoint that can be probed for liveness or quota headroom without performing a full inference call. Anthropic's public API has no documented /health or ping endpoint; the only live signal is a real or synthetic inference call, which carries cost, latency, and quota implications and is a new integration surface not present in the codebase today.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'Signals: … llm-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)'
scenarios: A probe that fires a real inference call to check liveness consumes quota and adds latency to every health-check cycle, creating its own load problem.
An implementation that uses a non-existent /health endpoint silently fails the check on every poll, making the signal always 'unknown' rather than meaningful.
Quota headroom cannot be read from a standard Anthropic REST endpoint without a real call or a separate quota-management API that is not documented publicly.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define the waiver authorization model in the plan (e.g. 'only members of the infra-oncall Gerrit group may waive; waiver requires a reason string; unauthorized attempts are rejected and logged') and update AC6 to include a negative test asserting unauthorized waiver is denied.
evidence: DESIGN mentions Gatekeeper as an analogy but does not define the actual role (e.g. 'repo admin', 'infra-oncall group', 'specific Gerrit group').
AC6: 'verified by a test exercising the waiver path and asserting the audit record is written' — tests only the happy path, not the guard.
Signal (4) missing persona: the admin/operator identity for waiver is unspecified.
findings.finding: The waiver/break-glass persona ('guard-the-guard on who may waive (Gatekeeper)') is referenced but the role or permission model is never defined. AC6 tests that 'the waiver path' works, but without specifying WHO can invoke it, the test cannot verify that unauthorized actors are denied — leaving the guard-the-guard protection untestable.
findings.location: DESIGN section, Waiver + break-glass bullet: 'guard-the-guard on who may waive (Gatekeeper)'; AC6

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State default values for RETRY_LIMIT (e.g. 3) and the thundering-herd replay window (e.g. spread re-runs over a 5-minute window, max N concurrent) in the plan so the executor can act without a round-trip.
evidence: RETRY_LIMIT appears twice with no value given.
'windowed (thundering-herd)' names the pattern but gives no window duration or max-concurrency figure.
AC3 asserts 'exactly one bounded re-run' — without a RETRY_LIMIT value, 'bounded' is untestable as a constraint.
findings.finding: RETRY_LIMIT is referenced as a bounding constraint ('bounded (RETRY_LIMIT)') and echoed in AC3, but no value or formula is stated. Similarly, the thundering-herd window size is referenced but undefined. These are defaultable gaps that an executor must invent.
findings.location: DESIGN section, Recovery bullet: 'bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd)'; AC3: 'bounded retry (RETRY_LIMIT)'
scenarios: Executor sets RETRY_LIMIT=1 (matching AC3's 'exactly one') but the design intent may have been 3 retries with exponential backoff.
Without a window definition, thundering-herd mitigation may be omitted entirely as 'unspecified'.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Recovery bullet, add: 'RETRY_LIMIT default: 3 attempts per recovery event; thundering-herd window: re-runs spread over 5 minutes with max 10 concurrent replays. These are configurable defaults.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the config revision identity scheme (e.g. 'the SHA of the applied Gerrit config ref' or 'a monotonic version counter stored alongside the config blob') so the AC4 test can unambiguously construct a stale-revision scenario.
evidence: AC4: 'Each health observation is bound to the config revision it was computed against and a stale observation is rejected rather than allowed to false-clear; verified by a test that presents a stale-revision observation and asserts rejection.'
No field name, type, or derivation protocol for 'config revision' is given anywhere in the plan.
This is a signal (2) implicit acceptance criterion — the data type/source of 'revision' is unstated.
findings.finding: The config-revision binding mechanism (AC4: 'each health observation is bound to the config revision it was computed against') is referenced but the revision identity scheme is never specified — no mention of whether it is a hash, a monotonic version counter, a timestamp, or a Gerrit change-id. A test asserting 'stale-revision rejection' cannot be written without knowing what constitutes a revision identifier.
findings.location: DESIGN section, Reliability bullet: 'marker bound to the config revision it was computed against'; AC4
scenarios: Executor chooses a wall-clock timestamp as the revision marker; a concurrent config push within the same second would not be detected as stale.
Executor chooses a git SHA; but config may not be git-tracked, making the binding impossible.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile AC3 with the DESIGN retry model: either restate AC3 as 'at most RETRY_LIMIT re-runs, with the first successful re-run replacing the stale vote' or confirm RETRY_LIMIT=1 per recovery event and update the DESIGN description accordingly.
evidence: DESIGN: 'bounded (RETRY_LIMIT)' — implies the retry count can be > 1.
AC3: 'asserts exactly one bounded re-run' — a test asserting exactly one re-run would FAIL if RETRY_LIMIT=3 and the system retries twice before succeeding.
The two sections give incompatible expectations for post-recovery behavior.
findings.finding: AC3 asserts 'exactly one bounded re-run' after recovery, but the DESIGN section specifies a retry loop bounded by RETRY_LIMIT (implying potentially multiple retries). If RETRY_LIMIT > 1, the design allows multiple re-runs per recovery event, directly contradicting AC3's 'exactly one' assertion.
findings.location: DESIGN Recovery bullet vs AC3
scenarios: Test passes with RETRY_LIMIT=1 but the design intent was 3; the implementation is under-specified and the test is over-constrained.
With RETRY_LIMIT=3 and the test asserting exactly one re-run, the test would fail on a correct implementation.
findings.suggested_fix: Revise AC3 to: 'On signal recovery a blocked review is automatically re-run; the system attempts at most RETRY_LIMIT times (default: 3), and the first successful re-run replaces the stale vote without human recheck; verified by a test that drives unhealthy→healthy and asserts re-run count ≤ RETRY_LIMIT and the stale vote is replaced.'

findings.finding: RETRY_LIMIT and the thundering-herd replay window size are asserted constants in the plan with no measurement basis or derivation plan. The detect-only pilot observes probe reliability but does not generate the load/timing data needed to choose safe values for these parameters.
findings.location: Design section ('bounded (RETRY_LIMIT), windowed (thundering-herd)')
scenarios: A RETRY_LIMIT that is too low (e.g., 1) causes premature exhaustion and terminal-alert storms during a rolling infra fix.
A replay window that is too narrow triggers thundering-herd on the LLM provider; too wide causes unacceptably long recovery latency.

evidence: Existing RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS covers llm-unavailable, review-error, scanner, gate-disabled — all infra-class signals
Plan names these same signals: 'LLM-provider (Anthropic reachable/quota)', 'environment'
A config-applied signal could be added as a new RETRYABLE_GAP_REASON without a new submit-requirement
Plan provides OSS rationale for the overall fail-closed stance but not for the specific choice of a new submit-requirement over extending the existing mechanism
findings.finding: The plan does not explain why a new dedicated Infra-Ready Gerrit submit-requirement is chosen over extending the existing retryable-gap mechanism (which already provides per-signal blocking, bounded retry, and auto-recovery via the reconciler). The existing RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS path is structurally very similar to what the plan proposes, is codebase-aligned, and would not require a new Gerrit label or project.config change. Without a positive rationale for the new gate over the existing mechanism, an implementer cannot justify the higher blast radius approach.
findings.location: DESIGN section: 'LANDING boundary — dedicated bot-cast Infra-Ready submit-requirement'
scenarios: Implementer adds both the new Infra-Ready gate AND keeps the existing RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS path, resulting in two overlapping infra-failure handling mechanisms with potentially inconsistent semantics.

The new submit-requirement is blocked by config-apply constraints (see prior finding), and the implementer falls back to the RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS extension anyway — having spent design effort on the submit-requirement approach.
findings.suggested_fix: If the core motivation is label separation (infra vs. content), state that explicitly: 'A new submit-requirement is required because extending RETRYABLE_GAP_REASONS leaves infra signals on the LLM-Review label, perpetuating the anti-pattern even with distinct tag vocabulary.' If that separation is not essential, consider the lower-blast-radius extension of the existing mechanism.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify that the 'per-signal message' for the Infra-Ready landing boundary is delivered via the robot comment on the Infra-Ready label vote (not via the submit-requirement description, which is a static project.config string in Gerrit 3.14.1); update AC2's test assertion to verify the message in the vote comment, not the submit-requirement.
evidence: Plan text: 'dedicated bot-cast Infra-Ready submit-requirement blocks submit with an explicit per-signal message'
infra/gerrit/project.config lines 162-166: [submit-requirement "LLM-Review"] carries only a static 'description' field; submittableIf is a label predicate, not a message surface
infra/gerrit/project.config line 9: 'a blocking label function is REJECTED on 3.14.1' — only submit-requirement predicates can block
src/rebar/review_bot/gerrit_client.py post_vote: robot_comments carry the dynamic message, but this is a label-vote comment, not a submit-requirement message

Evidence class: Contradicted — Gerrit submit-requirement descriptions are static config-file strings; the dynamic 'per-signal message' is only deliverable via the accompanying robot comment on the Infra-Ready label vote
findings.finding: The plan states the Infra-Ready landing boundary will 'block submit with an explicit per-signal message.' Gerrit's submit-requirement mechanism (the `[submit-requirement]` stanza in project.config) carries only a static `description` string — it has no mechanism to surface a dynamic, per-signal message at submit time. The only dynamic text available to a voter is the robot comment posted alongside the label vote itself. The plan conflates the submit-requirement's static description with a dynamic per-signal diagnostic message, which is a capability mismatch with the Gerrit 3.14.1 submit-requirement API surface.
findings.location: DESIGN section — 'LANDING boundary — dedicated bot-cast Infra-Ready submit-requirement blocks submit with an explicit per-signal message'
scenarios: An operator sees a blocked submit but the submit-requirement UI shows only the static description from project.config, not the per-signal reason (e.g. 'LLM quota exhausted' vs 'GitHub unreachable'). To get the per-signal reason they must read the robot comment on the change.

The plan's AC2 says 'Infra-Ready submit-requirement blocks submit with a per-signal message' — a test that checks for a dynamic per-signal message in the submit-requirement itself will always fail because no such surface exists in Gerrit's API.
findings.suggested_fix: In the DESIGN and AC2, replace 'submit-requirement blocks submit with an explicit per-signal message' with 'bot casts an Infra-Ready label vote with a per-signal robot comment; the [submit-requirement "Infra-Ready"] predicate references that label to block submit.' This matches how the existing LLM-Review gate works (static submit-requirement predicate + dynamic robot comment with the review message).
